SECRECY

Labels

Every byte string in a proof trace has a label, and every secrecy claim in DyLean is ultimately "this label is not corrupt unless something bad happened". A label is not a set of principals and not a level in a fixed lattice: it is a predicate on the execution trace that says when the bytes may be known by the attacker. This page builds up how labels are defined, combined, attached to bytes, and broken.

1 · A label is a corruption predicate

structure Label where
  isCorrupt: ExecTrace → Prop
  isCorruptLater: ∀ tr1 tr2, tr1 ≤ tr2 → isCorrupt tr1 → isCorrupt tr2
    := by grind

That is the whole definition. l.isCorrupt tr means "on this trace, bytes labelled l are allowed to be known by the attacker". The second field says corruption is permanent: once a label is corrupt, it stays corrupt on every extension. Two labels are equal when their predicates agree.

Labels are predicates on the execution trace, the one the attacker sees. Byte labels are computed from the proof trace, and their corruption is evaluated on tr.erase.

2 · canFlow: at most as secret as

def Label.canFlow (l1 l2: Label) (tr: ExecTrace) : Prop :=
  ∀ trLater, tr ≤ trLater → l2.isCorrupt trLater → l1.isCorrupt trLater

l1.canFlow l2 says: whenever l2 is corrupt, so is l1. Bytes labelled l1 may be handed to anyone allowed to know l2, because no information becomes available that was not already allowed.

The quantifier over later traces is deliberate. A plain implication at tr would be broken by a future compromise of l2 that did not compromise l1. Quantifying over every extension makes canFlow itself stable under trace growth, which is what lets it appear in invariants that are read back later.

3 · pub, secret, join, meet

def Label.pub    : Label := { isCorrupt tr := True }
def Label.secret : Label := { isCorrupt tr := False }
def Label.join (l1 l2: Label) : Label := { isCorrupt tr := l1.isCorrupt tr ∨ l2.isCorrupt tr }
def Label.meet (l1 l2: Label) : Label := { isCorrupt tr := l1.isCorrupt tr ∧ l2.isCorrupt tr }
secretnever corrupt: everything flows to it ↓ l₁.meet l₂corrupt only when both are: more secret than either ↓ l₁, l₂ ↓ l₁.join l₂corrupt when either is: less secret than either ↓ pubalways corrupt: flows to everything
Watch the names. In DyLean, join is the less secret combination: it is corrupt if either side is. Think of it as "the union of who may know". A value known to two parties, such as a DH shared secret, gets the join of their labels, because it leaks if either party leaks. meet is the more secret combination, used for a concatenation, which only leaks entirely if both halves do.
lemmastatement
joinIsCorrupt(l1.join l2).isCorrupt tr ↔ l1.isCorrupt tr ∨ l2.isCorrupt tr. This is the lemma that splits client_secrecy into two disjuncts
joinEql1.canFlow (l2.join l3) = (l1.canFlow l2 ∧ l1.canFlow l3)
meetEq(l1.meet l2).canFlow l3 = (l1.canFlow l3 ∧ l2.canFlow l3)
join_pub_leftpub.join l = pub
pubCanFlow, secret.canFlowpub flows to every label; every label flows to secret

4 · How bytes get labels

Bytes.label b tr is computed recursively over the structure of b. Each primitive contributes one rule, and #combine assembles them into one function.

Random bytes: the label is chosen

Fresh random bytes are the only leaves that carry an arbitrary label, and that label is not computed: it was recorded in the proof trace when the bytes were generated.

label := fun {timestamp, size := _} _rec tr =>
  match (tr.at? timestamp: Option ProofEntryT) with
  | some entry => entry.label       -- the ghost label written when genRand ran
  | none => Label.pub

The spec of genRand takes the label as a ghost argument, as a function of the generated bytes, so a label can mention the bytes' own public key: fun xSk => clientLabel me (dhPk xSk). Choosing a label is free. What it costs comes later: every place the bytes flow must be shown to respect it.

Derived bytes: the label is computed

termlabelwhy

Labels never change

theorem Bytes.label_later : tr1 ≤ tr2 → Bytes.WellFormed b tr1 → Bytes.label b tr1 = Bytes.label b tr2

A label is a fixed secrecy class decided when the bytes are made. For random bytes this holds because the entry at the timestamp never changes as the trace grows; every primitive must prove its rule preserves it. It is what lets an event invariant like k.label = clientLabel ⊔ serverLabel, proved at index 13, still be used by the secrecy theorem on a longer trace.

5 · Usages: what a key is for

A label says who may know bytes. A usage says what cryptographic role they play.

structure Usage where
  type: String
  tag: String
  data: Option Bytes

def Bytes.HasUsage (b: Bytes) (usg: Usage) (tr: ProofTrace) :=
  b.usage tr = usg ∨ (b.label tr).canFlow Label.pub tr.erase      -- public bytes have every usage

Like labels, usages are recorded for random bytes and computed otherwise; most constructors give Usage.nothing. Signatures check them: the honest case of a signature's invariant requires the key's usage to have type "SigKey", and passes the usage to the protocol's signing predicate. SignedDH's usage encodes the server's name, so the predicate can say which server signed:

def mkLongTermUsage (me: Participant) : Usage :=
  { type := "SigKey", tag := "SignedDH PKI", data := serialize ({ principal := me }: LongTermKeyUsage) }

6 · Publishable and KnowableBy

def Bytes.Publishable (b: Bytes) (tr: ProofTrace) := b.Invariant tr ∧ (b.label tr).canFlow Label.pub tr.erase
def Bytes.KnowableBy (l: Label) (b: Bytes) (tr: ProofTrace) := b.Invariant tr ∧ (b.label tr).canFlow l tr.erase

By canFlowPubEqIsCorrupt, "label flows to pub" is the same as "label is corrupt". So Publishable means: well-formed bytes whose label is already corrupt. Sending a message requires it. The central theorem goes the other way:

theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows_implies_Publishable : tr.Invariant → Bytes.AttackerKnows b tr.erase → b.Publishable tr

Anything the attacker knows has a corrupt label. Every secrecy theorem is this, plus an argument about which label the secret has and when that label is corrupt.

7 · How labels become corrupt

Protocol labels are built from events in the trace, almost always compromise events. The chain in SignedDH:

compromise 6attacker step →logs CompromiseEvent {Alice, {xPk, xSk}}in the trace →so LocalStateCompromised "Alice" {xPk, xSk}holds →so ClientEphemeralStateCompromised "Alice" xPkholds →= clientLabel "Alice" xPk is corrupt

The framework provides three label builders on top of events:

  • ProtocolEvent.label ev: corrupt once ev is logged.
  • PersistentLocalState.label p st: corrupt once that exact state of that participant is compromised. Compromisable states must show their contents are KnowableBy this label, which is how compromise can legally publish them. The state page has the details.
  • LongTermKeys.label name p pk: corrupt once the secret key behind pk is compromised.

8 · SignedDH's labels

def clientLabel (me: Participant) (xPk: Bytes) : Label where
  isCorrupt tr := ClientEphemeralStateCompromised me xPk tr
def serverLabel (me: Participant) (yPk: Bytes) : Label where
  isCorrupt tr := ServerEphemeralStateCompromised me yPk tr
  • xSk gets clientLabel me xPk and ySk gets serverLabel me yPk: each ephemeral secret is corrupt exactly when a state holding it leaks. Keying them by the public share makes them session-specific.
  • The signing nonce gets Label.secret. The signature invariant requires the signing key's label to flow to the nonce's label, because leaking a nonce can reveal the key; secret satisfies that for any key.
  • k = hash (dh xPk ySk), so by the hash and DH rules its label is clientLabel.join serverLabel: it leaks if either side's state leaks.

The theorem's three disjuncts come straight out of labels. If the attacker knows k, its label is corrupt. If the client's event invariant is in its honest case, that label is the join, and joinIsCorrupt splits it into "client state compromised" or "server state compromised". If it is in the other case, the server's long-term key label was corrupt before the event.

9 · Richer label designs in other examples

  • SignedDHKEM derives the session key from a DH secret and a KEM secret concatenated, so its label is a meet of two joins. Matching that, the theorem's disjunct is a conjunction: the attacker needs to break both halves. Its randomness labels also join in "this public key was broken" labels, modelling a primitive the attacker may break outright.
  • Ratchet uses labels that depend on when things happened, such as labelBeforeEvent: corrupt only if the long-term key was compromised before the receiver accepted an update. Such labels are how post-compromise security is stated.
